_comment: Preguntas ORIGINALES tipo NIE del capítulo 3.9. No son preguntas reales del examen. Comprueba con tu edición 2027.

questions.scenario: Which mental element is required for simple criminal damage (s. 1(1) CDA 1971)?
options: Intention or recklessness as to destroying or damaging the property

questions.scenario: Following R v G (2003), recklessness for criminal damage is…
options: Objective – what a reasonable person would have foreseen
Subjective – D was aware of a risk and it was unreasonable to take it

questions.scenario: Two boys, 11 and 12, set fire to newspapers behind a shop, not foreseeing the fire would spread. Following R v G, are they reckless as to the shop?
options: Yes – a reasonable adult would have foreseen it
No – they did not foresee the risk
Only if the shop was occupied

questions.scenario: Graffiti is sprayed with water-soluble paint that can be washed off. Is this 'damage'?
options: It can be – temporary impairment of value or usefulness and cost of cleaning (Hardman v CC Avon)

questions.scenario: Which of these is NOT 'property' under the CDA 1971?
options: A tamed fox kept as a pet
Wild mushrooms growing in a field

questions.scenario: A co-owner of a car deliberately smashes its windscreen. Can it be criminal damage?
options: Yes – property belongs to another if another person has a proprietary right or interest in it
Only if the other owner reports it

questions.scenario: What is the maximum penalty for simple criminal damage on indictment?
Criminal damage where the value of the damage is £5,000 or less (⚠) is…
Under s. 5(2)(a), a lawful excuse exists if D believed…
options: The person entitled to consent had consented or would have consented had they known the circumstances

questions.scenario: D, very drunk, breaks a window of a house believing it is his friend's house and that the friend would consent. It's actually a stranger's. Which is correct?
options: He may have a lawful excuse – the belief need only be honestly held, even if caused by intoxication (Jaggard v Dickinson)

questions.scenario: For s. 5(2)(b), the property protected must be believed to be…
options: In immediate need of protection, and the means adopted reasonable in all the circumstances

questions.scenario: Does the s. 5 lawful excuse defence apply to aggravated criminal damage (s. 1(2))?
D sets fire to his OWN house to claim insurance, reckless whether neighbours' lives are endangered. Which offence?
explanations: Own property not covered by s. 1(1).

questions.scenario: D fires a shotgun through a window at people inside; glass breaks. Following R v Steer, for s. 1(2) the danger to life must come from…
options: The destruction or damage to the property

questions.scenario: For aggravated criminal damage, must life actually be endangered?
options: No – intention or recklessness as to endangering life is enough
questions.manualRef: Blackstone's 2027 · 3.9 · Life need not be endangered

questions.scenario: What is the maximum penalty for arson?
D texts his ex: 'I'm going to smash up your car tonight', intending her to fear it will be done. He has no real plan. Which offence?
options: Threats to destroy or damage property (s. 2)

questions.scenario: For s. 2, what must D intend?
options: That the other would fear it would be carried out

questions.scenario: D is stopped carrying a hammer intending to break a shop window later. Which offence?
options: Possessing anything with intent to destroy or damage property (s. 3)

questions.scenario: Which offence carries 14 years: criminal damage that is…
Is erasing a computer file usually 'criminal damage'?
options: Generally no – unauthorised modification of data is covered by the Computer Misuse Act 1990

questions.scenario: A protester damages a fence at an airbase believing this will protect people's homes from a future nuclear war. Following R v Hill and Hall, is this 'in order to protect property'?
options: No – whether the act was done to protect property is judged objectively, and the threat was not immediate
Yes – honest belief is all that matters
Yes, if the means were reasonable
Only if the fence was cheap

questions.scenario: D breaks a neighbour's fence to rescue his dog that is being savaged. Possible defence?
options: Lawful excuse – protecting property (animal) believed in immediate need of protection, by reasonable means

questions.scenario: Wild flowers growing in a field are picked and trampled. Is this criminal damage?
options: No – flowers of plants growing wild are not property under the CDA
